name: Focusing illusion
statement: When a judgement about life as a whole is made with one aspect of it in focus, that aspect is given more weight than it carries in the lives being judged.
meaning: The claim is about the judge rather than the person judged. Schkade and Kahneman's 1998 argument runs in two steps. Someone living in a given circumstance attends to it at first and then attends mostly to other things, from meals to gossip. Someone imagining that circumstance holds it in view for the whole of the judgement. The two allocations of attention do not match, so the imagined life is dominated by the feature that distinguishes it. The paper states the prediction in general terms. Focus attention on any determinant of life satisfaction and its impact will be exaggerated. A footnote adds that focusing on things that matter makes the problem smaller. Wilson, Wheatley, Meyers, Gilbert and Axsom gave the same mechanism the name focalism in 2000, and their first footnote records that Schkade and Kahneman had independently called it a focusing illusion. That word travels in a second literature as well, where focalism means attending to an anchor, which the anchoring entry covers. Two neighbouring claims are separate. The impact bias is about how strongly and how long an event will move the person who lives through it, and belongs to affective forecasting. Duration neglect and the peak-end rule concern how a remembered episode is summarised. The focusing illusion is about the weight an attended feature gets inside a global evaluation.

origin.who: David A. Schkade and Daniel Kahneman
origin.note: Students in the Midwest and in southern California rated their own life satisfaction, or predicted the satisfaction of a student like themselves at a university in the other region. The paper names the illusion and ends on the line 'Nothing that you focus on will make as much difference as you think.'

evidence: The 1998 study ran 1,993 undergraduates at the University of Michigan (492), Ohio State (499), UCLA (503) and UC Irvine (499), recruited by survey firms and paid $7 to $10 for an hour. Satisfaction was rated from -5 to +5 and importance from 1 to 5. In the self condition the adjusted difference in overall life satisfaction between the regions was 0.01 and not reliable. Raw means for Caucasian respondents were 2.95 in the Midwest and 2.98 in California. Climate ratings were a different matter: adjusted differences favoured California by 4.03 on winter weather, 2.35 on overall climate and 0.88 on natural beauty, all p < .001. In the other condition both groups predicted a Californian would be more satisfied overall, by 0.57 for Midwestern respondents and 0.64 for Californian respondents, both p < .01. Self-reports also ran above predictions made for a similar person elsewhere, F(1, 1977) = 88.8, p < .001. Rating someone in a different region raised the importance placed on climate from 3.06 to 3.28, F(1, 870) = 16.2, p < .001. The predicted regional gap, F(1, 890) = 26.6, p < .001, disappeared when any of four climate items or cultural opportunities was entered as a mediator, each leaving p > .10. Half the sample was told the survey concerned the effect of climate on well-being, and that prime changed nothing. A separate item in the same paper asked 119 students about the moods of paraplegics. Those who had never known one put bad moods above good, 43% against 32%; those who had known one as a friend or relative reversed it, 20% against 53%. The 2006 Science paper applied the idea to income. Working women reported the share of the previous day spent in a bad mood, and another group predicted those shares for people in stated circumstances. Below $20,000 of household income the actual figure was 32.0% and above $100,000 it was 19.8%, a gap of 12.2 points from 64 and 59 respondents. Predictions for the same two groups were 57.7% and 25.7%, a gap of 32.0 points, p < 0.001. Among 740 women in Columbus, Ohio, household income correlated 0.32 with life satisfaction, 0.20 with the share of the day in a good mood and 0.06 with duration-weighted happiness, the last unmarked for significance.

replication.headline: The one direct repeat of the California study failed at one of the original sites, over two years and more than a thousand students, while manipulations of attention in the same experiment moved judgements as the theory says they should.
replication.detail: Ubel, Loewenstein and Jepson tested the California prediction in their Experiment 3, with 312 University of Michigan undergraduates of mean age 19.8, on the same -5 to +5 scale. Students rating a Michigan student gave 2.8. Students rating a UCLA student gave 2.7 and 2.5 before any intervention, differences of d = 0.02 and d = 0.13 in the wrong direction. Data were collected late in the autumn term, when the average daily high was 29 °F, with cloud on 80% and rain or snow on 7% of collection days. A footnote reports 747 Michigan students surveyed a year earlier with the same pattern, after which the authors obtained the original questionnaire and removed wording differences. Their sentence is 'We have no explanation for this failure.' The same experiment supported the mechanism from the other side. A defocusing exercise cut the within-subject California rating from 2.7 to 2.1, t = -3.26, p < .01, d = 0.28. A group rating only afterwards gave 1.7 against the other group's 2.7, t = 2.49, p < .05, d = 0.47. An adaptation exercise cut the within-subject rating from 2.5 to 1.8, t = -2.33, p < .05, d = 0.37, while its between-subject comparison was flat at 2.5. Their other two experiments split the mechanisms apart: defocusing left quality-of-life estimates for disability unchanged in 852 adults, and reflecting on adaptation raised them in 698 adults. Wilson and colleagues had already shown the attention manipulation working on forecasts. They studied 88 football fans at Virginia and Virginia Tech. Those who first filled in a diary of ordinary future activities made more moderate predictions about their happiness after the game, diary by outcome by time F(3, 255) = 4.23, p < .03. Aknin, Norton and Dunn asked 429 and then 315 Americans to place their own life satisfaction and to predict it at ten income levels. Predictions tracked the actual figures above median income and pulled far below them underneath it, against an actual income and happiness correlation of r = 0.11, p = 0.05.

study.cite: Ubel, P. A., Loewenstein, G., & Jepson, C. (2005). Disability and sunshine: Can hedonic predictions be improved by drawing attention to focusing illusions or emotional adaptation? Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 11(2), 111-123.

limits: No registered replication of the 1998 study was located, and no meta-analysis of the focusing illusion was located. Searches covered Crossref, general web search, and Europe PMC for 'focusing illusion' paired with replication, preregistration and life satisfaction terms. An OpenAlex sweep of the 880 works citing the 1998 paper was cut off by a rate limit after the citation count came back. The prediction gap in the 2006 income table has not been repeated in any study found here. The 1998 design compares different people rather than following the same ones, and everyone in it was an undergraduate at one of four universities. Nobody was tracked after moving. The income application has moved since 2006. Killingsworth collected 1,725,994 experience-sampling reports from 33,391 employed American adults and found experienced well-being rising with log income across the range, with no plateau above $75,000. In the adversarial reanalysis with Kahneman and Mellers, flattening above $100,000 appeared only in the least happy 15 to 20% of people, and happiness accelerated with income in the happiest 30%. That paper also puts the size of the whole relationship plainly. The correlation between average happiness and log income is 0.09 in the experience-sampling data. Medians at household incomes of $15,000 and $250,000 differ by about five points on a 100-point scale. Kahneman and Deaton's 2010 study could not be obtained and is described here from the 2023 reanalysis of it. Place is not inert either. Oswald and Wu fitted state effects to 1,213,992 responses to the 2005 to 2008 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, controlling for income and demographics. California's coefficient was -0.076, 95% CI -0.080 to -0.072, on a four-point satisfaction scale with Alabama fixed at zero. Kahneman's 2011 answer to the Edge annual question makes two further claims. Equalising incomes would shrink differences in life satisfaction by under 5%, and the mood advantage of high earners is about a third of what people expect. Neither figure carries a citation there, and neither was traced to a paper for this entry.
misreadings: The famous sentence is not in the paper it is credited to. The 1998 article closes with 'Nothing that you focus on will make as much difference as you think.' The 2006 Science paper quotes Schkade and Kahneman as writing 'Nothing in life is quite as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it', and that sentence appears nowhere in the 1998 text. The version in circulation is the title of Kahneman's answer to the 2011 Edge annual question, 'Nothing In Life Is As Important As You Think It Is, While You Are Thinking About It'. The California result is also narrower than its retellings. It is a comparison of undergraduates at four universities in one 1990s sample, not a finding about Californians, and the only direct attempt to repeat it did not. What the students got wrong was the overall judgement, not the climate. Midwestern students were in fact less satisfied with their winter weather, by 4.03 points on an 11-point scale. The illusion lies in how much that carried into a rating of life as a whole. The idea is not the same as hedonic adaptation, and Ubel's first two experiments show why the distinction earns its keep. Telling people to think about other parts of life left their disability estimates alone. Telling them to think about adapting changed those estimates. Focalism means one thing here and another in anchoring research, where it names attention to the anchor rather than to a life circumstance.
